explanations: In transfer(), the cache keys are deleted before COMMIT. Between the delete and the commit, a concurrent getBalance() misses the cache, reads the still-committed old row (READ COMMITTED cannot see the uncommitted update), and writes that old balance back into Redis with a 300 second TTL. After the commit nothing invalidates again, so customers and downstream checks see the pre-transfer balance for up to five minutes. Invalidation must happen after COMMIT succeeds (and ideally use a version check on set).

The ids are sorted and the SELECT ... ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE acquires both locks in the same global order, so no cycle can form. A rollback after a detected deadlock is recovery, not prevention; the UPDATE does wait on locks; separate clients are exactly what make lock conflicts possible.

BalanceCache.get() catches errors and returns null, so the code falls through to the database. But set() has no try/catch, so its rejection propagates out of getBalance() even though a valid balance was loaded. It does not return null for the account, set() does not swallow errors, and the TTL is unrelated to connection failures.

Both UPDATEs bump version and getBalance() copies it into the cached object, but BalanceCache.set() writes unconditionally and no query filters on version. Concurrency is handled by FOR UPDATE row locks, and expiry is handled only by the Redis TTL.
